summary.text: Coronis, pregnant by Apollo, took the mortal Ischys; the white raven that brought the news was turned black, and she died by Apollo's hand — or Artemis' — but her son was snatched from the pyre and reared by Chiron into the healer who raised the dead, until Zeus' thunderbolt struck him down. Epidaurus and Messenia told his birth otherwise, and his sons Machaon and Podalirius carried his art to Troy.

chapters.title: The raven's tidings
chapters.text: Apollo loved Coronis, daughter of Phlegyas, but against her father's will she went to live with a mortal, Ischys, the brother of Caeneus. Ovid calls her the loveliest girl in all Haemonia, Coronis of Larisa, dear to Phoebus as long as she stayed faithful — or unwatched. The god's bird, a raven still snow-white in those days, discovered the affair — Hyginus says Apollo had set it to guard the pregnant girl — and flew to tell its master. In Ovid a chattering crow tried to turn it back with her own story: she had told Minerva how Aglauros opened the chest that hid the infant Erichthonius, and lost the goddess's favour to the owl. The raven waved the omen aside.
chapters.citation: Apollod. 3.10.3; Ov. Met. 2.534–599; Hyg. Fab. 202, Astr. 2.40.2

chapters.title: The pyre
chapters.text: At the news the laurel slipped from Apollo's head. He bent his bow and drove an arrow through the breast he had so often held; dying, Coronis said she could have paid her penalty after the birth — now two would die in one. Too late the god repented, and when the pyre was lit he tore his son from the flames and the womb and carried him to Chiron. Hyginus makes Zeus' thunderbolt the death of Ischys — or, in his star-book, Apollo's arrows. Pausanias heard that Artemis killed Coronis to avenge the insult to her brother, and that Hermes snatched the infant from the burning pyre. The raven was cursed black, and Ovid bars it forever from the company of white birds.

chapters.title: Epidaurus and Messenia
chapters.text: Where, and to whom, he was born was disputed. Apollonius keeps the birth in Thessaly, at bright Lacereia by the Amyrus. The Epidaurians told Pausanias that Phlegyas came into the Peloponnese to spy out its strength, bringing his daughter, who hid that she carried Apollo's child. She bore a boy in their country and left him on the mountain now called Titthion, 'the Nipple'; a goat suckled him and the herd's dog kept watch, until the goatherd Aresthanas found him and drew back from the lightning that flashed from the child. Apollodorus names another mother first, Arsinoe daughter of Leucippus, and the Messenians claimed him as her son; but the Pythia, Pausanias says, answered that Coronis bore him in rocky Epidaurus.

chapters.title: Chiron's pupil
chapters.text: Chiron reared the god-born child and taught him healing and the chase. His prophetic daughter Ocyrhoe hailed the infant as the health-bringer of the world, who would give back souls already taken — until, daring it once against the gods' will, he was stopped by his grandfather's fire; for foretelling so much she was turned into a mare. Grown, he raised the dead, Apollodorus says, with the Gorgon's blood Athena gave him — the left veins' flow to destroy, the right's to save. Among the risen he names Hippolytus, Tyndareus and Glaucus son of Minos, and Hyginus credits him with Glaucus or Hippolytus — yet both authors elsewhere give Glaucus' revival to the seer who found the drowned boy. Hippolytus' return was remembered at Epidaurus, where an old slab recorded twenty horses he gave the god, and Ovid's Virbius owes his second life to the medicine of Apollo's son.

chapters.title: The thunderbolt
chapters.text: Zeus, fearing that men would learn the art from him and rescue one another, struck him with the thunderbolt; Hyginus makes the offence the raising of Glaucus or Hippolytus. Unable to strike at Zeus, Apollo killed the Cyclopes who had forged the bolt. Zeus would have hurled him into Tartarus, but at Leto's plea the sentence became a year's service to a mortal: Apollo herded the cattle of Admetus at Pherae. The Celts, Apollonius says, told another sequel — rebuked by his father, Apollo left heaven for the Hyperboreans, and the amber of the Eridanus is the tears he shed for Coronis' son. Hyginus counts Asclepius among the mortals made immortal, and his astronomers saw him in the Serpent-holder, set among the stars by Jupiter for Apollo's sake.

chapters.title: The sons and the serpent
chapters.text: In Homer, Asclepius is the peerless healer whose sons Podalirius and Machaon led thirty ships to Troy from Tricca and craggy Ithome. When Pandarus' arrow broke the truce, Machaon drew it from Menelaus, sucked the wound clean and spread on it the soothing drugs Chiron had once given his father in friendship. The god's own seat was Epidaurus, fount of his most famous sanctuaries, where Pausanias saw his image in gold and ivory with staff and serpent and a dog at its side, and slabs naming those he had healed. Ovid carries him to Rome: when plague wasted Latium, the god came from Epidaurus as a great serpent aboard the Roman ship, and on the island in the Tiber took his heavenly form again and ended the plague.
